title: Lean
summary: A block of Lean 4 that the author's computers verify, with Mathlib.
description: Proofs in the book are checked, not just shown. A Lean block is a Lean module of its own; blocks import each other by name, from any page. Only the author's computers run Lean: a phone writes and reads Lean blocks and shows what a computer found.

stories.as: an author writing about type theory
stories.want: the proofs in my book checked by Lean
stories.soThat: what the book claims is known to hold

stories.as: an author with an idea on the go
stories.want: to write a proof on my phone and have my computer verify it
stories.soThat: I can work on proofs anywhere and still know they hold

requirements.text: A Lean block holds Lean 4 source, which every device can write and read, highlighted as Lean.
A Lean block is a module with a name the author gives it, under `lean.module-root`; a Lean block on any page uses another by importing it, `import Book.<name>`.
A computer verifies a Lean block: whether it checks, its errors and warnings with their lines, and what commands such as `#eval` and `#check` print.
While the cursor is in a Lean block on a computer, the proof state at the cursor shows with the block.

A block's verdict is kept with the source it was reached for, and syncs: every device shows whether that source checked, with or without `sorry`, on which computer and when. A block whose source, or the source of a block it imports, changed since shows as not verified.
A computer verifies Lean blocks that changed on another device without the author opening them.
Phones never run Lean, and the app for phones carries none of it.
Lean blocks can import Mathlib, from a Lean workspace each computer keeps and sets up from Settings.
Typing a backslash abbreviation in a Lean block, such as `\to` or `\forall`, turns it into its symbol when the next character is typed, as in Lean's own editors.

values.description: The module every Lean block's module is under: a block named `Peano` is `Book.Peano`.
